title: feat(formula,objectql): read one hop through a lookup in a validation predicate
body:
Fixes #18682

Clause-②: yes

A validation rule can now read one hop through a lookup. `record.account.type` on an opportunity resolves the owning account's field instead of faulting with `runtime: No such key: type` — and because a broken validation is fail-closed, that fault previously rejected **every** write on the object, so the rule could not be authored at all.

## The shape

The engine statically analyses each predicate, learns exactly which reference fields it reads through and which related fields it names, loads those rows **before** evaluation, and binds them in place of the id. There is no `os.lookup(...)` / `os.exists` / `os.count` — those stay removed, and `packages/formula/src/eval-context-no-query-api.test.ts` stays green untouched. Every registered function is still pure once `now` is pinned.

**No new evaluation-context mechanism was added.** (⚠️ The sentence below describes the seam, not the authority: the read is a **system** read — see 「Read authority」 above.) The related rows arrive through the existing `record` root, hydrated by the engine exactly as it already hydrates a row for `$expand` readers and exactly as it already resolves `EvaluateRulesOptions.parent` and hands it over. `buildScope()` is untouched, so the CEL variable surface does not widen.

**One** deliberate difference from the `parent` precedent — ⚠️ this used to read 「two」, and the first of them no longer exists: after the maintainer's ruling both this read and `parent`'s are **system** reads, so that is now a similarity, not a difference:

- **Read authority — system, bounded by the projection.** The related rows are read under **system authority**, not the acting user. The read set is the fields the expression names, INTERSECTED with the related object's declared fields, plus `id` — computed in the engine before the query is built, so an elevated read can never carry a column the predicate did not name. A validation rule's output is a pass/fail the system enforces; the related value never reaches the caller, and the refusal names the reference field, the related object, the named column and the rule, ⛔ never the value. ⚠️ The accepted cost, stated rather than buried: a caller can **infer** a value they cannot read by observing which writes are refused. That inference channel was accepted knowingly and is kept as narrow as it was — nothing makes the refusal more informative than 'this rule refused this write'. (Ruled on card #18682; the earlier acting-user reading is superseded, because it made the rule unauthorable for the very persona it exists to constrain.)
- **The dry run carries the same bound — ⚠️ and at this head it does NOT carry it completely.** `engine.validate()` previews a write without performing one, and resolves related rows only for a caller who could perform that write. ⛔ **An earlier version of this line claimed the check is 「the same evaluator and permission sets the CRUD gate itself uses, not a second decision about who may write」. The at-tier review measured that false** (record `5780579159`): the probe implements `isSystem`, `userId`, resolution-failure deny and the CRUD grant, while the write gate also composes ADR-0066 D3 capability and ADR-0090 D10 delegation. Two caller classes therefore still reach an elevated read through the preview that the write path refuses outright — a D3 caller holding `allowCreate` without the capability (reachable via `POST /data/:object/import` `dryRun:true`), and an `onBehalfOf` naming a dangling delegator. ⇒ **This is an open blocking finding, not a shipped property.** The repair is to make the probe the write twin of the plugin's existing `canReadObject` and pin it by equivalence against the registered middleware, as that method already is.
- an unresolved row is left **absent** on purpose. No id, the row gone, or the read threw — each leaves the field unbound and the write is **rejected** — ⚠️ at this head by a **discriminated binding refused before evaluation**, ⛔ not by a fault raised during it (same outcome, different mechanism; the earlier wording described the mechanism this PR no longer uses). Never silently true, and never silently false. ⚠️ 「refused by the security layer」 was listed here as a fourth cause and has been removed: under a system-authority read it cannot occur, so naming it described a path that does not exist.

Hydration is **per rule** and onto a **copy**. Per rule, because hydrating a field replaces its stored id with the related record and a sibling rule comparing the bare id must keep seeing the id. Onto a copy, because the record handed to a rule is the real write payload — hydrating it in place would send the expanded object to the driver in place of the foreign key.

## Two shapes refused at authoring time

Both fault at evaluation today, so neither removes anything that works — the refusal replaces a per-row runtime fault with one loud message naming the repair:

| Shape | Write instead |
| --- | --- |
| a reference field read both through the relationship and as a plain value | `record.account.id` for the value comparison |
| a read deeper than one hop | denormalise onto the related object, or read it in a hook |

Gated on `fieldTypes`, which is what tells a reference field from an object-valued one: `record.address.city` traverses today and keeps traversing.

## Scope

Object validation rules (`script` / `cross_field`) only — and the system-authority read is confined to that one seam: `resolvePredicateRelated` is called from the validation seams alone, so the elevation cannot reach an RLS or UI predicate. The field-level `requiredWhen` / `readonlyWhen` / option `visibleWhen` predicates fail **open** and are deliberately out; RLS predicates are out; depth is one hop.

## Acceptance

`docs/qa/platform-checklist/areas/records-forms.json` gains `records-forms.predicate-relationship-traversal`, covering the three ruled outcomes, plus a dogfood case on the showcase app: `showcase_invoice` now refuses an invoice against a churned account **on the server**. Its `account` picker already scoped churned accounts out of the dropdown, which is exactly why the rule earns its place — a picker filter is a UI affordance, not a server guarantee, and REST, imports, flows and agents never touch the picker.

## Acceptance notes

- `PredicateRule.fields` is read by the runtime (`checkPredicate` derives the violation's field from `rule.fields?.[0]`) but the spec's `script` rule schema **refuses** the key — authoring one is an `unrecognized_keys` parse error, which is how the showcase rule first failed. So for authored rules that read is always `undefined` and the violation always attributes to `_record`. Noted, not filed and not fixed here: it is inert rather than harmful, and it is not this card's surface.
